cards.title: The 'Human Hijacks' Checklist for Ad Creative and Landing Hooks
cards.summary: Seven recurring psychological levers (make it about them, event, demonstration, proof, daily behavior, dream, rebel) that creators like Clemens use to make product messaging stop the scroll.
cards.use_when: You're writing the hook, headline or first seconds of a video ad, advertorial or landing page and need a menu of angles to test.
steps: List the seven hijacks: (1) Make it about them — lead with the customer's benefit, not your product. (2) Make it an event — 'nothing attracts a crowd like a crowd'. (3) Powerful demonstration — PT Barnum's elephant, the axe, the sword through the bullet, the dirty-water demo; show dramatic, near-shocking proof instead of stating a feature. (4) Unquestionable proof — doctors, named experts, influencers, someone willing to literally stand in the elevator being cut. (5) Change a daily behavior — bolt your product onto something they already do (in their coffee, at breakfast) or create a new daily ritual. (6) Sell the dream — the outcome in vivid, specific personal terms. (7) Help them be a rebel or feel superior — give them the badge and the tool to stick it to 'the man'.
Source argues each of these can change a company's trajectory on its own, so generate several angle variants and test rather than picking one.
caveats: Demonstration and proof claims must be truthful for your product; Clemens describes tactics like deliberately baiting a video with ASMR before revealing the product, which carries real brand-trust and platform-policy risk if overdone.
'Rebel' and 'superiority' framings require care in regulated or mainstream categories.

cards.title: Hijack Existing High-View Attention Formats (the ASMR Remix)
cards.summary: Find a proven high-view organic format, replicate its opening, then swap in your product at the payoff moment.
cards.use_when: You need a cheap, high-retention video hook for paid social and want to borrow a format that already has proven viewership.
steps: Scan TikTok/Reels/Shorts for oddly-satisfying formats with very large view counts (Clemens cites glass bottles full of marbles rolling down concrete stairs, which he says routinely hit ~10 million views).
Identify the exact sensory/hook mechanics — here, the sound of glass rolling, the clink on each stair, then the crack and the marble cascade.
Shoot the same opening so it reads as that format, then 'hijack' the video at the natural payoff moment (the smash) and reveal your product.
Clemens' team reported far higher watch-through doing this than starting on the product, and they describe the technique candidly as 'a complete bait and switch'.
caveats: Clemens himself calls it a bait and switch — using someone else's format can damage trust, invite negative comments and risk platform or IP complaints.
The retention benefit is the presenter's reported experience, not a guaranteed benchmark.
Verify current ad-platform policies on misleading creatives.

cards.title: Lead With a Problem the Market Already Cares About When the Category Is Unknown
cards.summary: If buyers don't know your product category, open on a pain they already feel and educate them into the category from there.
cards.use_when: You're launching a product in a category buyers have never heard of, so a benefit statement does nothing.
steps: In Clemens' 'Clueless' market stage, he argues you must create the marketing wave yourself: the audience knows nothing about the product.

Open on the familiar symptom instead. For probiotics he started with digestive issues and bathroom irregularity — things people already cared about — and only then explained the microbiome and the product as the aid.

Build a 'bigger villain' into the story so the uncomfortable symptom has an external cause. In the probiotic case: hidden sugars and artificial sweeteners in foods labelled healthy, plus alleged suppressed studies (a paid livestock-sugar experiment where cows died; aspartame tested on animals with claimed falsified tumour reports).

Position your product as the simple daily fix to that villain. His Keybiotics presentation reportedly reached 100M+ views in roughly four months and birthed the biggest probiotic brand of the time — treat that as an illustrative case, not a promise.
caveats: Villain narratives must be factually defensible; Clemens is repeating claims about food and sweetener companies, so don't restate them as your own without verification.
Reaching that volume required major organic and celebrity amplification that can't be planned.

cards.title: Diagnose Your Market Stage Before Writing Copy: Clueless, Curious, Saturated
cards.summary: The message that works depends on whether the market has never heard of the product, has heard of it, or is fully saturated.
cards.use_when: You're setting copy strategy for a product launch, relaunch or ad refresh and need to know which kind of hook is viable.
steps: Clueless stage (nobody knows the category): You must create the marketing wave. Lead with the related pain or symptom the audience already feels, not the category term. Clemens' 2013-14 probiotic ads opened on digestive health.

Curious stage (audience knows the term but not the detail): You can 'jump right' in and use a counter-intuitive hook that presumes knowledge. His 2018 headline: 'Doctor says throw your probiotics in the trash' — it only works because the reader already believes probiotics are good, then the page explains most probiotics lack the right strains and that prebiotics matter.

Saturated stage (category commoditised): Clemens says the probiotic market is here now and he is not launching new probiotics; at conferences he tells would-be entrants 'good luck'. Breakthrough still happens, but requires a strong campaign rather than category education.
caveats: These three stages are Clemens' own heuristic from his Twitter thread, not a measured formula; validate against your own search and survey data.
The stage can be different for your sub-niche than for the whole category.

cards.title: Read Your Market Stage Off Branded Search Trends
cards.summary: Category-level search curves show when education campaigns are creating demand and when the market matures.
cards.use_when: You want evidence of whether your category is clueless, curious or saturated before committing to messaging or spend.
steps: Track the category search term (e.g. 'probiotics') over years, not months, and overlay your brand and spokesperson terms.

Clemens notes the category trend visibly spiked after their education-led campaign, dropped the day they were kicked off Google, then recovered with the next brand — and spiked again when Dr. Gundry campaigns ran, with 'Gundry' searches rising on days campaigns were strongest.

If your brand or spokesperson term tracks the campaign bursts, your education is creating the category wave; if the category curve is flat or above your brand's, buyer knowledge already exists and you can use 'curious'-stage hooks.

Historical analogue: he points to cigarette search-interest spiking after the Easter Day parade and VW Beetle after 'Think Small' — attribution caveat aside, the pattern is demand created by campaigns.
caveats: Search interest is a proxy for attention, not sales; cross-check with revenue and new-customer data.
Attribution between campaign and trend cannot be proven from the curve alone.

cards.title: Pick the Awareness Stage, Then Choose the Headline Type
cards.summary: Match your headline to what the reader already knows: symptom-first for unaware buyers, contrarian category-claim for aware buyers.
cards.use_when: You're choosing between a problem-led and a contrarian headline on a PDP, advertorial or landing page.
steps: For unaware audiences: use a symptom or consequence headline that presumes nothing about your category, then teach. Clemens used 'digestive health' framing in early probiotic ads.

For aware audiences: use a pattern-interrupt that contradicts a belief they already hold — 'throw your probiotics in the trash' — and deliver the counter-explanation on the page (not enough strains, prebiotics matter, etc.).
The contrarian headline only converts if the reader has a prior belief to disrupt; on a clueless audience it reads as nonsense.
Keep the proof and dream elements of the seven hijacks after the headline: the page still needs demonstration, believable proof and a vivid outcome.
caveats: Clemens' examples are his own campaigns; timing and performance aren't transferable as benchmarks.
Contrarian claims may be scrutinised by ad platforms and regulators — keep them defensible.

cards.title: Turn the Buying Ritual Into a Daily Habit Hook
cards.summary: Attach your product to a behaviour the customer already performs each day, or give them a new daily ritual, so repeat use and retention follow.
cards.use_when: You're designing the offer, bundle or PDP benefit copy for a consumable or supplement and want repeat purchase built into the message.
steps: Identify an existing daily moment you can bolt onto — Clemens cites Bulletproof-style 'add this to your coffee', or swapping a light breakfast for a hearty one.
Alternatively create the ritual: for probiotics the strategy was to encourage taking something every day, which also builds the replenishment/subscription habit.
Write the PDP and ad copy around that moment ('add it to your morning coffee', 'take it with breakfast') rather than around the product alone.
Support the habit with a fulfilment and replenishment design that matches the daily cadence — subscribe-and-save intervals, reminders, pack sizes that fit the ritual.
caveats: Daily-use positioning raises regulatory and substantiation requirements for supplement-type claims.
Habit framing works best for products genuinely consumed daily; forcing it on occasional-use products can feel dishonest.
